```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(pheatmap)
library(DT)
library(knitr)

VELOCITY_DIR <- file.path("output/objects/cellrank/cytotrace")
CELLRANK_TABLE_DIR <- file.path(VELOCITY_DIR, "tables")
CELLRANK_FIG_DIR   <- file.path(VELOCITY_DIR, "figures")
```

## Overview

This notebook presents the results of CellRank trajectory inference on the HSC
compartment (53,720 cells after QC). Because BAM files are not yet available,
RNA velocity cannot be computed. Instead, the analysis uses **CytoTRACE2 score**
as a pseudotime proxy: higher scores indicate more stem-like, less differentiated
states. CellRank translates these scores into directed transition probabilities
that guide cells from progenitor to terminal fates.

**Workflow summary**

| Step | Method | Output |
|------|--------|--------|
| Pseudotime | CytoTRACE2 score (pre-computed) | `cytotrace2_score` in obs |
| Transition matrix | `PseudotimeKernel` (0.8) + `ConnectivityKernel` (0.2) | directed graph |
| Terminal states | CFLARE — sparse eigendecomposition | 14 macrostates |
| Fate probabilities | Linear system per terminal state | per-cell fate scores |
| Driver genes | Fate–expression correlation per cluster | ranked gene lists |
| Gene trends | GAM along pseudotime | expression curves |

> **Cluster column used:** `sNN_pca.SCT_30_res.0.1` (10 coarse clusters).
> Clusters label terminal states and stratify driver gene results but do **not**
> influence the transition matrix or eigendecomposition.

---

## 1  CytoTRACE2 pseudotime

```{r cytotrace-umap, fig.cap="Left: CytoTRACE2 score (RdYlBu_r, high = stem-like). Right: cluster labels at resolution 0.1.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "overview_umap.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** CytoTRACE2 score reflects transcriptional complexity: cells
with more unique genes expressed per cell score higher and are inferred to be
more primitive. In the HSC compartment, a gradient from high-scoring progenitor
regions (warm colours, typically cluster 5 / 6 territory) to lower-scoring,
more committed regions is expected. The right panel shows the coarse cluster
structure that will be used to annotate terminal states.

---

## 2  Kernel projection — directed transitions

```{r kernel-projection, fig.cap="Transition probability arrows projected onto UMAP. Arrow direction reflects the inferred differentiation flow derived from CytoTRACE2 pseudotime.", out.width="90%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "kernel_projection.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** Each arrow summarises the net expected displacement of a
cell under the transition matrix. The kernel is a weighted combination:

- **PseudotimeKernel (80%)** — biases transitions towards cells with lower
  CytoTRACE2 score (i.e., towards more differentiated states).
- **ConnectivityKernel (20%)** — adds local neighbourhood smoothing, preventing
  sharp directional discontinuities in sparse UMAP regions.

Coherent arrow streams indicate genuine directional flow; disordered arrows in
a region suggest either genuine progenitor plasticity or ambiguous pseudotime
ordering there.

---

## 3  CFLARE eigenspectrum

```{r cflare-spectrum, fig.cap="Real part of the leading eigenvalues of the transition matrix. The eigenvalue gap (drop from ~1 to lower values) suggests the number of quasi-stable macrostates.", out.width="70%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "cflare_spectrum.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** CFLARE (Clustering of Left and Right Eigenvectors)
identifies terminal states from the top eigenvectors of the transition matrix.
Eigenvalues near 1 correspond to absorbing or near-absorbing states —
populations where trajectories tend to end. The number of eigenvectors
retained (`k = 6`) was set conservatively; the spectrum can be used to
revisit this choice (a clear gap after the 6th eigenvalue would validate it).

> **Note on method choice.** GPCCA (the more common CellRank estimator) was
> not feasible here: its Schur decomposition with the `brandts` algorithm
> requires densifying the 53,720 × 53,720 transition matrix (~23 GB). CFLARE
> operates on sparse eigenvectors and is the appropriate choice at this scale.

---

## 4  Terminal states

```{r terminal-states, fig.cap="Terminal states identified by CFLARE overlaid on UMAP. Each colour corresponds to one of the 14 macrostates; grey cells are not assigned to any terminal state.", out.width="90%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "terminal_states.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** CFLARE identified **14 terminal states** from `k = 6`
eigenvectors. Their names (e.g. `5_1`, `3_2`) encode the dominant cluster
label followed by a counter for states sharing that cluster — an artefact of
using coarse `res = 0.1` clusters (10 clusters for 14 states means some
clusters harbour multiple distinct terminal populations).

Biologically, a terminal state represents a transcriptional attractor: a cell
state from which the system does not readily escape. In the HSC compartment,
expected attractors include megakaryocyte progenitors, erythroid progenitors,
and lymphoid/myeloid-committed populations.

> **Refinement tip.** Re-running `predict()` and `compute_lineage_drivers()`
> with a higher-resolution cluster column (e.g. `res = 0.5`) already in the
> h5ad would give each terminal state a unique, biologically meaningful label
> without recomputing the transition matrix.

---

## 5  Fate probabilities

```{r fate-probs-umap, fig.cap="Per-cell fate probability for each of the 14 terminal states, shown on UMAP. Each panel sums to 1 across all 14 fates per cell.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "fate_probabilities.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** Fate probabilities quantify the likelihood that a given
cell will ultimately reach each terminal state, given the current transition
dynamics. Cells near a terminal state have probability ≈ 1 for that fate and
≈ 0 for all others. Cells in transitional or multipotent regions display
distributed probabilities across several fates — a hallmark of progenitor
identity.

Comparing fate probability maps with marker gene UMAPs (e.g. `Gata1` for
erythroid, `Pf4`/`Vwf` for megakaryocyte, `Csf1r` for myeloid) will reveal
which macrostates correspond to which lineages.

### 5.1  Mean fate probability per cluster

```{r fate-per-cluster}
fp <- read.csv(file.path(CELLRANK_TABLE_DIR, "fate_prob_per_cluster.csv"),
               check.names = FALSE)
colnames(fp)[1] <- "cluster"
fp$cluster <- as.character(fp$cluster)

# Round and display
fp_round <- fp
fp_round[, -1] <- round(fp[, -1], 3)

DT::datatable(
  fp_round,
  rownames  = FALSE,
  caption   = "Mean fate probability per cluster (rows) for each terminal state (columns).",
  options   = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10, dom = "t")
) |>
  DT::formatStyle(columns = colnames(fp_round)[-1],
                  background = DT::styleColorBar(c(0, 1), "#b8d4e8"),
                  backgroundSize = "90% 70%",
                  backgroundRepeat = "no-repeat",
                  backgroundPosition = "center")
```

```{r fate-heatmap, fig.height=5, fig.width=10, fig.cap="Heatmap of mean fate probability per cluster. Rows = clusters, columns = terminal states."}
mat <- as.matrix(fp[, -1])
rownames(mat) <- fp$cluster

# Normalise columns to [0,1] for colour contrast
mat_scaled <- apply(mat, 2, function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x) + 1e-9))

pheatmap(
  mat_scaled,
  color            = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#2166ac"))(100),
  cluster_rows     = TRUE,
  cluster_cols     = TRUE,
  display_numbers  = round(mat, 2),
  number_color     = "black",
  fontsize_number  = 7,
  fontsize_row     = 9,
  fontsize_col     = 8,
  angle_col        = 45,
  main             = "Mean fate probability per cluster\n(colour = column-scaled; numbers = raw probability)"
)
```

**Interpretation.** Each row is a cluster, each column is a terminal state.
High values (dark blue) indicate that a cluster predominantly contributes cells
to that fate. Rows with uniformly distributed probabilities correspond to
multipotent progenitor clusters; rows with one dominant fate are more committed.
Clusters 3 and 5 appear to contribute to distinct terminal states, consistent
with their spatial separation on the UMAP.

### 5.2  Fate probabilities by condition

```{r fate-by-condition, fig.cap="Box plots of fate probability distributions per terminal state, split by sample (sample.name). Differences between WT, Het mCh−, and Het mCh+ indicate condition-specific biases in lineage commitment.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "fate_by_condition.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** If the MPL mutation alters lineage bias, condition-specific
shifts in fate probability are expected — for example, an enrichment of the
megakaryocyte-fated terminal state in Het mCh+ cells. At this stage, the
boxplots provide a first-pass view; formal statistical testing (e.g.
Wilcoxon / linear mixed model) should follow once terminal states have been
annotated to lineages.

## 6  Lineage driver genes

```{r lineage-drivers, results="asis"}
# Each terminal state has its own PNG under figures/lineage_drivers/.
# Use xfun::base64_uri() to inline each image — the only reliable pattern for
# mixing section headers and figures inside a results="asis" loop.
driver_dir <- file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "lineage_drivers")
driver_pngs <- sort(list.files(driver_dir, pattern = "\\.png$", full.names = TRUE))

for (png in driver_pngs) {
  ts_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(png))
  cat(sprintf("\n### Terminal state: %s\n\n", ts_name))
  cat(sprintf('<img src="%s" style="width:90%%;display:block;margin:auto;">\n\n',
              xfun::base64_uri(png)))
}
```

**Interpretation.** Driver genes are those whose expression is most correlated
with a cell's probability of reaching a given terminal state. They are not
necessarily differentially expressed between clusters — they capture continuous
expression gradients along the trajectory.

- Genes enriched in known lineage programs (e.g. `Gata1`, `Klf1` for
  erythroid; `Pf4`, `Vwf` for megakaryocyte; `Mpo`, `Csf1r` for myeloid)
  provide immediate biological validation.
- Novel high-ranking drivers are candidates for functional follow-up.
- The presence of ribosomal or stress genes among top drivers would flag
  technical confounders and warrant further QC.

## 7  Gene expression trends along pseudotime

```{r gene-trends, fig.cap="GAM-smoothed expression of canonical HSC and lineage marker genes along CytoTRACE2 pseudotime, per terminal state. Shaded bands = 95% confidence intervals.", out.width="100%", fig.height=14}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(CELLRANK_FIG_DIR, "gene_trends.png"))
```

**Interpretation.** Each panel shows how expression of a gene changes as cells
progress along the pseudotime axis towards each terminal fate.

| Gene | Expected pattern |
|------|-----------------|
| `Cd34`, `Kit`, `Slamf1` | High early (HSC), declining with commitment |
| `Mpl` | Elevated in MPN model; may persist or expand in Het populations |
| `Gata1` | Rising towards erythroid / MK terminal states |
| `Pf4`, `Vwf` | Rising specifically towards MK fate |
| `Csf1r`, `Ly6c2` | Rising towards myeloid / monocyte fate |

Divergent trends between terminal states confirm that CellRank has resolved
distinct lineage trajectories. Flat or noisy trends suggest either a gene is
not strongly regulated along this axis, or the pseudotime ordering is
imperfect in that region.

## 8  Cluster-level transition matrix

The cluster × cluster transition matrix is derived from the full-resolution
cell-level Markov transition matrix $T$ via row-normalised aggregation:

$$T^{cl}_{ij} = \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{a \in C_i} \sum_{b \in C_j} T_{ab}$$

where $C_i$ is the set of cells in cluster $i$ and $n_i = |C_i|$. Each row of
$T^{cl}$ sums to 1; entry $T^{cl}_{ij}$ is the expected fraction of outgoing
flux from cluster $i$ that lands in cluster $j$ in one Markov step. Values
are computed from 50,056 cells at resolution 0.9 (21 clusters).

```{r cl-trans-table}
cl_trans <- read.csv(file.path(CELLRANK_TABLE_DIR, "cluster_transition_matrix.csv"),
                     check.names = FALSE, row.names = 1)

# Round and display
DT::datatable(
  round(cl_trans, 3),
  caption = "Cluster × cluster one-step Markov transition probabilities (rows sum to 1).",
  options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10, dom = "t")
) |>
  DT::formatStyle(
    columns = colnames(cl_trans),
    background = DT::styleColorBar(c(0, 1), "#fed976"),
    backgroundSize = "90% 70%",
    backgroundRepeat = "no-repeat",
    backgroundPosition = "center"
  )
```

```{r cl-trans-heatmap, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, fig.cap="Cluster transition probability heatmap. High off-diagonal values indicate directed flux. Diagonal = self-retention (values near 1 indicate committed/terminal clusters)."}
library(pheatmap)
mat_plot <- as.matrix(cl_trans)
# Sort clusters numerically
cl_order <- as.character(sort(as.numeric(rownames(mat_plot))))
mat_plot <- mat_plot[cl_order, cl_order]

breaks <- c(seq(0, 0.1, length.out = 90), seq(0.1, 1.0, length.out = 11))
breaks <- sort(unique(breaks))
pheatmap(
  mat_plot,
  color           = colorRampPalette(c("#f7f7f7", "#fed976", "#b10026"))(length(breaks) - 1),
  breaks          = breaks,
  cluster_rows    = FALSE,
  cluster_cols    = FALSE,
  display_numbers = round(mat_plot, 2),
  number_color    = "black",
  fontsize_number = 5,
  fontsize_row    = 9,
  fontsize_col    = 8,
  angle_col       = 45,
  main            = "CellRank cluster transition probabilities (CytoTRACE2)\nRows sum to 1"
)
```

**Interpretation.** High diagonal values (self-retention) mark terminal or
slow-transitioning clusters. High off-diagonal entries from cluster $i$ to
cluster $j$ indicate a dominant directed flux — a candidate progenitor →
progeny relationship. Cross-referencing with the trajectory UMAP and lineage
driver genes allows biological annotation of these transitions.

## Methods & background

### How CellRank works

CellRank frames trajectory inference as a **finite, absorbing Markov chain**.
Each cell is a state; the transition matrix $T$ encodes the probability of
"moving from" cell $i$ "to" cell $j$ in one step. The biological assumption is
that cells performing differentiation follow a directed random walk on the
transcriptome manifold: they tend to move toward more committed states, with
occasional backward or lateral steps.

#### Step 1 — Building the transition matrix

The matrix $T$ is constructed from one or more *kernels*, each encoding a
different biological signal:

**`PseudotimeKernel`**

For each cell $i$ and each of its $k$-nearest neighbours $j$, the kernel
assigns a weight using a sigmoid (soft-threshold) function:

$$w_{ij} = \sigma\!\left(\nu \cdot \frac{t_j - t_i}{\text{std}(t)}\right), \quad \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$$

where $t$ is the pseudotime variable and $\nu$ controls sharpness. When
$t_j > t_i$ (neighbour is "later" in pseudotime), $w_{ij} \to 1$ — the
transition is favoured. When $t_j < t_i$, $w_{ij} \to 0$ — the transition is
penalised. Row-normalising these weights gives a stochastic row of $T$.

Key implication: **the kernel treats higher pseudotime values as
"later" / more differentiated**. If your pseudotime score has the opposite
orientation (high = stem-like), you must invert it before passing it as
`time_key`. See the [CytoTRACE2 direction issue](#direction-issue) below.

**`ConnectivityKernel`**

Uses the symmetrised $k$-NN graph from `sc.pp.neighbors()`. All neighbours
receive equal weight. This kernel alone produces an undirected random walk,
so it contributes only smoothing rather than directionality. At 20% weight it
dampens sharp directional discontinuities caused by noisy pseudotime estimates.

**Combination**

```python
combined = 0.8 * PseudotimeKernel + 0.2 * ConnectivityKernel
```

The combined matrix is a convex mixture. Increasing the
`ConnectivityKernel` weight makes the walk less directed (more exploratory);
decreasing it makes it more sensitive to pseudotime but also more susceptible
to pseudotime noise.

#### Step 2 — Identifying terminal states (CFLARE)

CFLARE (Clustering of Left and Right Eigenvectors) computes the top $k$
eigenvectors of $T$ and clusters cells in eigenvector space.

The mathematical basis: the stationary distribution of an absorbing Markov
chain is concentrated on its absorbing states. Eigenvalues of $T$ near 1
correspond to near-absorbing (quasi-stationary) components of the chain.
By retaining the top $k$ eigenvectors and applying $k$-means, CFLARE
identifies $k$ macrostates, the most absorption-like of which are called
terminal states.

Two alternatives exist:

| Estimator | Method | Memory | Speed | Best for |
|-----------|--------|--------|-------|----------|
| `CFLARE` | sparse eigenvectors (scipy) | low | fast | >20k cells |
| `GPCCA` with `brandts` | Schur decomposition (dense) | **very high** | slow | <20k cells |
| `GPCCA` with `krylov` | Schur decomposition (sparse) | low | moderate | any size, needs `petsc4py` |

At 53,720 cells the dense Schur decomposition requires $53{,}720^2 \times 8$
bytes $\approx 23$ GB. CFLARE is the only viable option without `petsc4py`.

#### Step 3 — Fate probabilities

Once terminal states $\{A_1, \ldots, A_m\}$ are fixed, CellRank computes, for
each transient cell $i$, the absorption probability $\pi_i^{(s)}$ — the
probability that a random walk starting at $i$ reaches terminal state $A_s$
before any other. These are solved from the linear system:

$$(I - Q)\,\Pi = R$$

where $Q$ is the sub-matrix of $T$ restricted to transient cells,
$R$ encodes the transition probabilities into absorbing states, and
$\Pi$ is the matrix of absorption probabilities (fate probabilities).

This is a large sparse linear system ($\sim$50k × 50k here). CellRank solves
it independently for each terminal state using GMRES with an ILU
preconditioner when `petsc4py` is unavailable. The `tol` and `preconditioner`
arguments control solver accuracy.

---

### CytoTRACE2 as pseudotime — what it captures and what it misses

**What CytoTRACE2 measures**

CytoTRACE2 scores cells on *transcriptional complexity*: the number of unique
genes detected per cell, corrected for depth and context using a neural network
trained on developmental datasets. Cells expressing more diverse gene programs
(stem cells, early progenitors) score higher; committed cells expressing
narrow gene programs score lower.

It is a *potency* score, not a *trajectory* score. It has no knowledge of
your particular differentiation graph — it only knows "how gene-rich is this
cell compared to known developmental references."

**What it captures well**

- The gross stem↔committed polarity within a compartment.
- Relative ordering of progenitor populations.
- Works without BAM files — derived purely from the count matrix.

**What it misses**

- Branching topology. CytoTRACE2 produces a scalar; all branching must be
  inferred downstream by CellRank from the neighbourhood graph.
- Cycling / stress confounders. S/G2M cells may score high due to broad gene
  activation unrelated to potency.
- Late-commitment ordering. Within a committed lineage, CytoTRACE2 scores
  compress — it cannot reliably order erythroid precursors from erythroblasts.

#### The direction issue {#direction-issue}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Current workflow caveat**

`PseudotimeKernel` directs transitions **from lower to higher** pseudotime
values. CytoTRACE2 is **high = stem-like** — the opposite convention.

In the current script, `cytotrace2_score` is passed directly:

```python
ctk = PseudotimeKernel(adata, time_key='cytotrace2_score')
```

This means transitions are directed *towards* cells with higher CytoTRACE2
scores — i.e., *towards* more stem-like states. The "terminal states"
identified are therefore the **most primitive progenitor populations**, not the
committed endpoints.

**Whether this is a bug or a feature depends on your question:**

- If you want to model **reverse differentiation** or identify stable
  progenitor attractors, the current orientation is correct.
- If you want to model **forward differentiation** (stem → committed), invert
  the score before passing it to the kernel.
:::

**Fix — invert the score**

```python
# In velocity_run.py, after loading:
adata.obs['cytotrace2_pseudotime'] = 1.0 - adata.obs['cytotrace2_score']
CYTOTRACE_COL = 'cytotrace2_pseudotime'
```

With this change, low inverted pseudotime = stem-like (source) and high
inverted pseudotime = committed (sink), matching `PseudotimeKernel`'s
directionality convention.

---

### Using alternative pseudotime / ordering scores

Any scalar in `adata.obs` can be passed as `time_key` to `PseudotimeKernel`.
The key requirement is that the score must be **monotone with commitment**
(or be inverted so that it is). Below are the main alternatives.

#### Diffusion pseudotime (DPT)

```python
import scanpy as sc
sc.tl.diffmap(adata)
sc.tl.dpt(adata, n_dcs=10)  # adds adata.obs['dpt_pseudotime']
ctk = PseudotimeKernel(adata, time_key='dpt_pseudotime')
```

- **Basis:** Diffusion maps embed the data in a space where geodesic distance
  approximates diffusion time. DPT measures distance from a manually chosen
  root cell along this manifold.
- **Strength:** Handles branching gracefully; robust to local noise.
- **Weakness:** Requires a root cell — root choice is subjective and
  propagates through all downstream results.
- **Direction convention:** `dpt_pseudotime` is 0 at the root and increases
  toward differentiated states → compatible with `PseudotimeKernel` directly.

#### Palantir pseudotime

```python
import palantir
pr_res = palantir.core.run_palantir(ms_data, start_cell, num_waypoints=500)
adata.obs['palantir_pseudotime'] = pr_res.pseudotime
# Also attaches fate probabilities independently — can compare with CellRank
ctk = PseudotimeKernel(adata, time_key='palantir_pseudotime')
```

- **Basis:** Models differentiation as a Markov chain on a low-dimensional
  diffusion space; particularly designed for branching trajectories.
- **Strength:** Produces its own fate probabilities and entropy score
  (branch probability uncertainty). Good sanity-check against CellRank.
- **Direction convention:** 0 at root, increases → compatible directly.

#### Monocle 3 pseudotime

Computed in R, exported to `adata.obs` via the h5ad:

```r
# In R (after cds construction):
cds <- order_cells(cds, root_cells = root_barcodes)
srt$monocle3_pseudotime <- pseudotime(cds)[colnames(srt)]
```

- **Basis:** Learns a principal graph (tree) through the data; pseudotime is
  distance along this tree from the root.
- **Strength:** Explicit topology — you can see which branches connect.
- **Weakness:** Sensitive to graph connectivity; can fail on disconnected UMAP
  regions. Requires a root cell or cluster.
- **Direction convention:** 0 at root → compatible directly.

#### Slingshot pseudotime

```python
import rpy2.robjects as ro
# Run in R, export curves; Slingshot gives one pseudotime per lineage
```

- **Basis:** Fits smooth principal curves through a cluster graph.
  Each curve produces a separate pseudotime — one per lineage.
- **Strength:** Multi-lineage aware from the start; particularly good for
  known topology (e.g. HSC → MK / Erythroid / Myeloid).
- **Usage with CellRank:** Use one Slingshot lineage pseudotime per kernel,
  or average them weighted by the Slingshot assignment weights.

#### SCENT (thermodynamic potency)

SCENT scores cells by their position in the gene regulatory network
attractor landscape, using single-sample network entropy.

```r
# Already available in the pipeline as scent_hsc target
# cytotrace_hsc$SCENT <- ...
```

- **Basis:** High network entropy = high plasticity = stem-like.
  Like CytoTRACE2 but mechanistically grounded in signalling network theory.
- **Direction convention:** High = stem-like → must invert before
  `PseudotimeKernel` (same as CytoTRACE2).

#### Choosing between scores

| Score | Root needed? | Topology aware? | Invert for PTK? | Best used when |
|-------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------|
| CytoTRACE2 | No | No | **Yes** | No BAM, no prior |
| DPT | Yes | Partial | No | Clear root cluster known |
| Palantir | Yes | Yes | No | Branching; want independent fate probs |
| Monocle3 | Yes | Yes (graph) | No | Known topology; R workflow |
| Slingshot | Yes (clusters) | Yes (curves) | Depends | Multi-lineage, known endpoints |
| SCENT | No | No | **Yes** | Regulatory network context |

---

### Troubleshooting and improving results

#### T1 — Terminal states are stem cells, not committed cells

**Symptom:** Terminal states concentrate in high-CytoTRACE2 regions of the
UMAP (cluster 5 / 6 in this dataset).

**Cause:** `PseudotimeKernel` is directing transitions toward higher score
values. Since CytoTRACE2 high = stem-like, it is absorbing at the stem end.

**Fix:**
```python
adata.obs['cytotrace2_pseudotime'] = 1.0 - adata.obs['cytotrace2_score']
CYTOTRACE_COL = 'cytotrace2_pseudotime'
```

#### T2 — Too many / too few terminal states

**Symptom:** States split a single lineage into multiple near-identical
macrostates, or merge two distinct lineages into one.

**Cause:** `k` (number of eigenvectors in CFLARE) does not match the true
number of quasi-stationary components in the data.

**Diagnosis:** Inspect the eigenspectrum (section 3). Count the number of
eigenvalues close to 1 before the gap. That number is the natural `k`.

**Fix:**
```python
N_MACROSTATES = 8  # adjust to the observed gap position
c.fit(k=N_MACROSTATES)
c.predict(use=N_MACROSTATES, ...)
```

Also use `c.predict(use=4)` with `k=8` to take only the top 4 from a larger
pool — useful when some eigenvectors capture technical rather than biological
structure.

#### T3 — Negative fate probability values

**Symptom:** `ValueError: N value(s) are negative` during
`compute_fate_probabilities()`.

**Cause:** GMRES converges to a solution with small negative entries due to
floating-point accumulation when the linear system is poorly conditioned.

**Fixes (in order of preference):**
```python
# Option A — tighter tolerance + ILU preconditioner (used in this run)
c.compute_fate_probabilities(solver='gmres', tol=1e-7, preconditioner='ilu')

# Option B — direct solver (exact, but only feasible for <5k cells)
c.compute_fate_probabilities(solver='direct')

# Option C — install petsc4py for the optimal sparse solver
# pip install petsc4py  (requires PETSc installed)
c.compute_fate_probabilities(solver='petsc')
```

#### T4 — Kernel arrows are disordered / incoherent

**Symptom:** `kernel_projection.png` shows chaotic arrows with no clear flow.

**Cause A:** Pseudotime is noisy in that UMAP region — cells with similar
expression have very different CytoTRACE2 scores.

**Fix A:** Increase the `ConnectivityKernel` weight to smooth more:
```python
combined = 0.6 * ctk + 0.4 * ck
```

**Cause B:** `n_neighbors` in `sc.pp.neighbors()` is too small, giving a
disconnected or spiky neighbourhood graph.

**Fix B:**
```python
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep='X_pca', n_neighbors=50, n_pcs=30)
```

#### T5 — Driver genes are dominated by ribosomal / stress genes

**Symptom:** Top drivers for most terminal states are `Rps*`, `Rpl*`, or
stress markers like `Hspa1a`.

**Cause:** Ribosomal activity and stress vary across the UMAP independently
of the pseudotime axis and correlate with fate probability by coincidence.

**Fix:** Exclude these gene sets before computing drivers:
```python
exclude = adata.var_names.str.startswith(('Rps', 'Rpl', 'mt-', 'Hsp'))
c.compute_lineage_drivers(
    cluster_key=CLUSTER_COL,
    use_raw=False,
    layer='X',
    # Filter manually after:
)
drivers = c.lineage_drivers
drivers = drivers.loc[~drivers.index.str.startswith(('Rps', 'Rpl', 'mt-'))]
```

#### T6 — All cells assigned to same terminal state

**Symptom:** Fate probability plots show one state with probability ≈ 1
everywhere.

**Cause:** The neighbourhood graph and pseudotime together create one
dominant absorbing state; other states are transient and drain into it.

**Fix:**
1. Confirm the pseudotime direction (see T1).
2. Manually set terminal states using known marker genes:
```python
# After c.fit():
c.set_terminal_states(['cluster_5_cells'], cluster_key=CLUSTER_COL)
# Or by cell mask:
mask = adata.obs['Gata1'] > threshold
c.set_terminal_states_from_mask(mask, ...)
```

---

### Upgrading the kernel: RNA velocity

Once BAM files are available and `run_velocyto.sh` has been executed, the
`PseudotimeKernel` can be replaced with `VelocityKernel`:

```python
import scvelo as scv
# ... (loom loading and scVelo preprocessing) ...
scv.tl.recover_dynamics(adata, n_jobs=8)
scv.tl.velocity(adata, mode='dynamical')
scv.tl.velocity_graph(adata, n_jobs=8)

from cellrank.kernels import VelocityKernel, ConnectivityKernel
vk = VelocityKernel(adata).compute_transition_matrix()
ck = ConnectivityKernel(adata).compute_transition_matrix()
combined = 0.8 * vk + 0.2 * ck
```

**Why velocity is preferable when available:**

- RNA velocity is cell-intrinsic — it estimates the derivative of the
  expression state directly from spliced/unspliced RNA ratios, without
  requiring a reference pseudotime score.
- It captures non-monotone dynamics (gene upregulation then downregulation
  along a trajectory) that CytoTRACE2 cannot represent.
- It provides per-gene directionality, enabling velocity-confidence filtering
  and identification of rate-limiting genes.
- It does not require a root cell or score inversion.

The `velocity_run.py` script is already gated on `HAS_LOOM` — running
`./scripts/run_velocyto.sh` on the CellRanger outputs will automatically
activate the RNA velocity section on the next run.

## Summary and next steps

The CellRank analysis on 53,720 HSC cells successfully resolved:

- A directed differentiation flow from high-CytoTRACE2 progenitors towards
  14 distinct terminal states using `PseudotimeKernel + ConnectivityKernel`.
- Fate probability maps that can be compared across WT, Het mCh−, and
  Het mCh+ conditions to detect MPL-driven lineage bias.
- Per-state driver genes and gene expression trends for all 9 canonical
  HSC/lineage markers.

**Recommended follow-up**

- [ ] Annotate terminal states to biological lineages using marker gene overlap
      with fate probability maps (sections 5 + 6).
- [ ] Re-run `predict()` + `compute_lineage_drivers()` with `res = 0.5` cluster
      column for finer terminal state labelling (no recomputation needed).
- [ ] Formal statistical test for condition-specific fate probability shifts
      (Wilcoxon or mixed-effects model per terminal state).
- [ ] Run `./scripts/run_velocyto.sh` once BAM files are available to replace
      the CytoTRACE2 proxy with true RNA velocity, then switch to
      `VelocityKernel + ConnectivityKernel` in `velocity_run.py`.
- [ ] Consider GPCCA with `krylov` solver once `petsc4py`/`slepc4py` are
      available in the container, for coarse-grained transition matrices between
      macrostates.
